Is Pine River upstream of Blue Creek? Can water from Pine River reach Blue Creek through the stated network?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Rewrite the facts as arrows: North Fork→Willow Stream, Pine River→Willow Stream, Willow Stream→Blue Creek. 2. Follow arrows starting from Pine River. 3. An arrow path reaches Blue Creek, so Pine River is upstream of Blue Creek.

Directed graph; edge X→Y means water can flow from X to Y; query reachability.

G4. Neighbours and borders
Problem 266. Crossing the fictional border network of Oak
Knowledge context.
Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.
Given facts.

Countries are represented by the fictional states Oak, Riverbend, Meadow, Willow, Northfield, Cedar. Shared borders: Oak–Riverbend, Riverbend–Meadow, Meadow–Willow, Oak–Northfield, Northfield–Cedar, Cedar–Willow.
Rules.
Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.
Task.
What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Oak to Willow? Is Riverbend necessarily crossed?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Turn each shared border into an undirected link. 2. A shortest-link search gives distance 3 from Oak to Willow. 3. Remove Riverbend and check whether Willow is still reachable from Oak. 4. It is still reachable, so Riverbend is not unavoidable.
Answer.
3 border crossing(s); Riverbend is not unavoidable.
Knowledge takeaway.
Neighbourhood on a map is a graph relation; shortest routes and unavoidable transit points are different questions.
Formal model.
Undirected graph; shortest path length plus reachability after deleting a candidate vertex.

G5. Maps, legends, and clues
Problem 271. Reading a layered map legend (A1)
Knowledge context.
A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.
Given facts.

Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has forest, river, road; B2 has road, village. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.
Rules.

A cell satisfies the task only if it has every required attribute. Extra attributes do not disqualify it unless the task says so. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.
Task.
Which cell or cells satisfy all of these conditions: forest, road? Explain by intersecting the clues. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Convert the requested symbols into the attribute set ['forest', 'road']. 2. Check each cell for every required attribute. 3. The matching set is ['A1', 'B1']. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.
